concepts.definition: A visual design pattern that provides simultaneous access to both detailed view of a selected region (focus) and surrounding information (context) within a single display, reducing cognitive load during exploration of large graphs.
key_refs: Munzner (2000) / Interactive Visualization of Large Graphs and Networks
Furnas (1986) / Generalized Fisheye Views
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's metro-map interaction should use focus+context (e.g., highlighted stations/neighborhoods + surrounding context) to let users zoom deeply into subgraphs without losing spatial orientation or overview context.

concepts.definition: Interaction paradigm enabling users to directly interact with visual objects (drag, resize, filter) rather than typing commands, reducing abstraction layers and improving perceived control and feedback.
key_refs: Shneiderman (1992) / Tree Visualization with Tree-Maps: 2-D Space-Filling Approach
Norman (2013) / The Design of Everyday Things
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must prioritize drag-and-drop node repositioning, click-to-filter edges, and gestural pan/zoom over command-line queries; avoids the 'flight to chat' anti-pattern by keeping control in the user's hands via visual affordances.

concepts.definition: Non-linear magnification technique applying smooth scaling gradients from a focal point, compressing peripheral areas while magnifying focus region to show both detail and context in continuous space without jarring discontinuities.
key_refs: Furnas (1986) / Generalized Fisheye Views
Sarkar & Brown (1994) / Graphical Fisheye Views
concepts.implication: MetroGraph could employ fisheye lensing on dense graph regions to prevent node/edge clutter while allowing users to see local neighborhoods without multiple zoom levels; smooths the interaction cost vs. visual clarity trade-off.

concepts.definition: Formal framework (Furnas) computing importance scores for graph nodes based on distance from user's focus, structural properties, and user-specified weights; enables principled selective rendering and progressive disclosure.
key_refs: Furnas (1986) / Generalized Fisheye Views
Perer (2009) / Search, Show Context, Expand on Demand: Supporting Large Graph Exploration with Degree-of-Interest
concepts.implication: MetroGraph can formalize node/edge visibility decisions using DOI: nodes close to selected subway stations show full detail, distant regions collapse to abstract clusters; prevents visual overload while maintaining navigability.

concepts.definition: Non-Euclidean space embedding using 3D hyperbolic geometry to achieve exponential space expansion, enabling efficient visualization of tree-like graphs with 100K+ nodes via radial focus+context projection while maintaining graph topology.
key_refs: Munzner & Burchard (1995) / H3: Laying Out Large Directed Graphs in 3D Hyperbolic Space
concepts.implication: While hyperbolic geometry is specialized, its principle applies to MetroGraph: use layout algorithms (force-directed, hierarchical) that allocate exponentially more space to focused regions, allowing massive graphs to scale without extreme zoom factors.

concepts.definition: Automatic visual perception occurring in ~200ms before conscious attention, leveraging parallel processing of visual features (color, orientation, size) to enable rapid pattern recognition without active cognitive effort.
key_refs: Attneave (1954) / Some Informational Aspects of Visual Perception
Triesman & Gelade (1980) / A Feature-Integration Theory of Attention
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's visual design should use distinct colors, shapes, or saturations for node types (database tables, workflow steps, agents) to enable instant recognition without requiring conscious attention; improves visual query performance and reduces cognitive load.

concepts.definition: Seven fundamental visual dimensions (position, size, value, texture, color, orientation, shape) used to encode data attributes; provides principled basis for assigning data dimensions to visual properties according to data type and task requirements.
key_refs: Bertin (1967) / Semiology of Graphics
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's design should assign graph attributes to visual variables systematically: node position encodes spatial proximity/layout, color encodes data type/category, size encodes importance/degree, ensuring consistent and perceptually effective encoding.

concepts.definition: Empirical ranking of visual encoding effectiveness for quantitative judgment (Cleveland & McGill 1984): position > length > angle > area > slope > color saturation; guides choice of visual variables for task-specific data encoding.
key_refs: Cleveland & McGill (1984) / Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should prioritize horizontal/vertical position for encoding critical graph properties (node rank, importance), avoid area/color for quantitative comparisons where position could work, ensuring users can accurately interpret graph relationships.

concepts.definition: Design principles for node-link layouts including edge crossing minimization, uniform edge lengths, symmetry preservation, and clustering; empirically shown to improve user comprehension and task performance (Purchase et al.).
key_refs: Purchase (1997) / Cognitive Measurements of Graph Aesthetics
Purchase et al. (2001) / Empirical Evaluation of Graph Drawing Aesthetics
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's layout algorithms must minimize edge crossings, maintain symmetry, and balance edge lengths to improve visual clarity; use automated readability metrics (edge crossing counts, node occlusion) during layout generation.

concepts.definition: Physics-inspired iterative algorithm treating nodes as charged particles and edges as springs, converging to equilibrium via velocity Verlet integration; produces aesthetically pleasing layouts with minimal edge crossings and balanced spacing.
key_refs: Fruchterman & Reingold (1991) / Graph Drawing by Force-Directed Placement
D3 Force-Directed Graph Layout implementation
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should use force-directed or similar iterative algorithms for interactive layout refinement, allowing users to drag nodes while forces auto-arrange neighbors; combines user control with algorithmic guidance.

concepts.definition: Technique reducing visual clutter in dense graphs by routing similar/nearby edges along common paths, revealing aggregate flow patterns and high-level connectivity structure while suppressing low-level edge details.
key_refs: Holten (2006) / Hierarchical Edge Bundling for Visualization of Large Graphs
Holten et al. (2017) / Force-Directed Edge Bundling
concepts.implication: MetroGraph could apply edge bundling to dense workflow/agent graphs, grouping edges by destination or relationship type to reveal macro-patterns; enables pattern discovery without node repositioning.

concepts.definition: Progressive disclosure technique changing visual representation at different zoom levels: at low zoom, nodes aggregate into clusters with summary statistics; at high zoom, individual nodes and attributes appear; prevents visual overload while enabling detail-on-demand.
key_refs: Perlin & Fox (1993) / Pad: An Alternative Approach to the Computer Interface
Bederson & Hollan (1994) / Pad++: A Zoomable Graphical Sketchpad
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's zoom levels should transition smoothly between abstraction levels: zoom-out shows data lineage as colored arrows between tables; zoom-in reveals individual fields, transforms, and metadata; prevents overwhelming users while allowing deep exploration.

concepts.definition: Multi-level representation strategy organizing graph nodes into nested clusters at increasing levels of abstraction, enabling navigation from high-level overview to granular details; supports summarization, filtering, and progressive refinement.
key_refs: Munzner (2000) / Interactive Visualization of Large Graphs and Networks
Balzer & Deussen (2005) / Level-of-Detail Visualization
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should organize graphs hierarchically: Databases > Tables > Fields, Workflows > Steps > Tasks, Agents > Components; users explore via expand/collapse, with aggregated view showing summary statistics (table row counts, execution times).

concepts.definition: Two complementary graph representations: node-link diagrams excel at topology/path tasks and spatial understanding; adjacency matrices excel at density/connectivity assessment and scaled to larger graphs; hybrid approaches combine strengths.
key_refs: Ghoniem et al. (2004) / Matrices or Node-Link Diagrams: Which Visual Representation is Better for Visualising Connectivity Models?
Henry & Fekete (2006) / MatrixExplorer: A Dual-Representation System for Exploring Structured Relations
concepts.implication: MetroGraph could offer dual views: node-link diagram for intuitive data lineage navigation; adjacency matrix for dense dependency analysis; linked brushing between views surfaces different insights (topology vs. connectivity patterns).

concepts.definition: Interaction technique enabling coordinated selection across multiple linked views: selection in one view (e.g., highlighting nodes) automatically highlights corresponding elements in complementary views, enabling rapid cross-view pattern discovery.
key_refs: Becker & Cleveland (1987) / Brushing Scatterplots
Roberts (2007) / State of the Art: Coordinated and Multiple Views in Exploratory Visualization
concepts.implication: MetroGraph could highlight workflow execution traces across node-link diagram and timeline view; clicking a table in the graph highlights all upstream/downstream tables and their dependencies across multiple linked views.

concepts.definition: Cognitive model (Pirolli & Card 1999) describing how users navigate information spaces via scent cues (indicators of relevance); users adaptively choose paths balancing information scent density with search cost, forming exploration strategies.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card (1999) / Information Foraging in Information Access Environments
Chi & Pirolli (2007) / Rational Analyses of Information Foraging
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must provide strong information scent: node labels, preview popups on hover, color-coded edge types (dependencies, transforms, etc.) guide users toward relevant tables/workflows without requiring exhaustive search.

concepts.definition: Visual cues (e.g., mini-previews in widget controls, node color, edge labels) signaling content relevance and reducing uncertainty about navigation outcomes; strong scent improves search efficiency and reduces cognitive load.
key_refs: Chi & Pirolli (2007) / Rational Analyses of Information Foraging on the Web
Olston & Chi (2003) / ScentTrails: Integrating Browsing and Searching on the Web
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should embed scent cues: hovering over a table shows record count, column names; hovering over a workflow shows execution status, average runtime; edge labels indicate join conditions or transformation types.

concepts.definition: Iterative cognitive process (evidence → hypotheses → schemas) in which users formulate interpretations from information fragments via cycles of search (evidence foraging), synthesis, and schema building; visualization supports rapid hypothesis-evidence cycles.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card (2005) / The Sensemaking Process and Leverage Points for Analyst Technology
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's interaction must support rapid hypothesis testing: users should easily explore 'what if I remove this table?' (filter), 'where does this transform apply?' (highlight), 'how many rows flow through this step?' (aggregation) — enabling iterative schema refinement.

concepts.definition: Cognitive principle that users develop spatial mental models of graph layouts; preserving relative node positions during dynamic updates (filtering, editing) enables faster re-recognition and reduces disorientation.
key_refs: Misue et al. (1995) / Layout Adjustment and the Mental Map
Purchase et al. (2007) / Animation, Small Multiples, and the Effect of Mental Map Preservation
concepts.implication: When filtering MetroGraph's graph (e.g., hiding completed workflows), remaining nodes should stay in place rather than re-layout; animated transitions between states preserve user's spatial mental model, reducing cognitive disruption.

concepts.definition: Smooth interpolation between graph states (layout changes, filtering, highlighting) with staged animations and visual continuity; improves perception of object correspondence and enables users to track changing elements.
key_refs: Heer & Robertson (2007) / Animated Transitions in Statistical Data Graphics
Lin & Dunne (2018) / Common Fate for Animated Transitions
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's pan/zoom/filter operations should use smooth animations (200-500ms) rather than instant changes; animating both movement (edges/nodes) and appearance (opacity fades) helps users track state changes and maintain spatial orientation.

concepts.definition: Direct-manipulation interfaces enabling end-users to construct queries via visual means (dragging nodes, clicking edges, selecting attributes) rather than text syntax; improves accessibility and encourages exploratory querying.
key_refs: Catarci et al. (1997) / Visual Query Systems: A Perspective
Soutou (2017) / GraphTQL: A Visual Query System for Graph Databases
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should enable visual query construction: users drag two tables onto canvas to define a join; right-click to add filter conditions; edge labels auto-suggest join columns; avoids SQL syntax while enabling complex queries through visual composition.

concepts.definition: Visual or interactive cues (color, shape, border, cursor changes) signaling actionable properties of interface elements; strong affordances improve discoverability by making possible interactions obvious without explicit instruction.
key_refs: Norman (2013) / The Design of Everyday Things
Saffer (2009) / Designing Gestural Interfaces
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's nodes should show clear affordances: draggable nodes have cursor change on hover, clickable nodes show hand cursor, contextual menu buttons appear on selection; reduces need for documentation while guiding intuitive interaction.

concepts.definition: Design principle ensuring interactive capabilities are visible and learnable without requiring external documentation; achieved through consistent affordances, progressive disclosure, and contextual help.
key_refs: Nielsen & Norman (2000) / Information Architecture and Usability
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must avoid hidden features: interaction capabilities should be visible (drag handles on nodes, right-click menu labels), progressive disclosure reveals advanced options (on hover or submenu), enabling users to self-discover features.

concepts.definition: Graph structures with multiple levels of hierarchy (nodes contain sub-nodes) or clustering (nodes grouped into super-nodes); requires specialized visualization combining node-link diagrams at multiple abstraction levels with edge bundling across hierarchy levels.
key_refs: Eades & Feng (1997) / Compound Graph Visualization
Sander & Scholl (2005) / Orthogonal Hypergraph Layout
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's data lineage graphs are inherently hierarchical (schemas > tables > fields, workflows > stages > tasks); support expand/collapse of compound nodes, with inter-level edges showing cross-hierarchy relationships.

concepts.definition: Hardware-accelerated techniques (GPU rendering, spatial indexing, level-of-detail culling) enabling interactive pan/zoom of millions of nodes/edges; essential for maintaining 60+ FPS responsiveness on large datasets.
key_refs: Munzner (2000) / Guaranteed Frame-Rate Drawing
Li et al. (2019) / Deck.gl: Large-scale Web-based Visual Analytics Made Easy
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should use WebGL or similar GPU acceleration, spatial indexing for culling off-screen nodes, and level-of-detail rendering (simplify node shapes at small zoom) to enable smooth interaction with 100K+ node graphs.

concepts.definition: Algorithmic techniques aggregating nodes/edges into summary supergraphs while preserving macro-structure; reduces graph complexity for visualization and analysis while enabling drill-down to original granularity.
key_refs: Navlakha et al. (2008) / Graph Summarization with Bounded Error
concepts.implication: MetroGraph could summarize large data lineage graphs: multiple related tables aggregate into 'table clusters', multiple pipeline stages collapse into macro-steps; users explore via expand/collapse, revealing detail on demand.

concepts.definition: Techniques for visualizing graphs that change over time: animation (showing change via frame sequences), small multiples (side-by-side snapshots), or hybrid approaches; must preserve mental map while showing temporal evolution.
key_refs: Beck et al. (2015) / A Taxonomy and Survey of Dynamic Graph Visualization
concepts.implication: MetroGraph could visualize workflow execution evolution: animation shows task progression over time, or side-by-side snapshots (small multiples) show pipeline state at different timestamps; enables understanding of dynamic behavior.

concepts.definition: Specialized interaction techniques enabling efficient navigation of very large graphs: search/filter (reduce visible nodes), focus+context (zoom while preserving overview), aggregation (collapse similar nodes), and progressive refinement.
key_refs: Munzner (2000) / Interactive Visualization of Large Graphs and Networks
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must support scalable interaction: users should search/filter by table name, workflow status, or dependency type to reduce graph size; focus+context keeps orientation; aggregation collapses unrelated nodes; enables exploring enterprise-scale data lineage.
